sections.title: Intermediate Concept: Quadratic Inequalities
sections.content: In banking and competitive exams, you are rarely asked just to find roots. You are given two equations (one in x, one in y) and must compare their roots to choose among 5 options: 1) x > y, 2) x < y, 3) x ≥ y, 4) x ≤ y, 5) x = y or Relationship Cannot Be Established (CND).

sections.title: The Comparison Matrix
sections.content: To compare x and y, you must compare EVERY root of x with EVERY root of y. If x has roots x1, x2 and y has roots y1, y2, you do 4 comparisons: x1 vs y1, x1 vs y2, x2 vs y1, x2 vs y2. All comparisons must point in the same direction to give a definite answer.

sections.title: The 'Cannot Be Determined' (CND) Scenario
sections.content: If during your 4 comparisons, you get opposing signs (e.g., x1 > y1 but x2 < y2), the relationship cannot be established. The answer is instantly CND.

sections.title: Coefficient Balancing (Cross-Multiplication)
sections.content: When comparing roots, dividing by 'a' can create messy decimals. Instead, cross-multiply the 'a' coefficients. Multiply the roots of x by the 'a' of equation y, and multiply the roots of y by the 'a' of equation x.

sections.title: Visualizing the Number Line
sections.content: When roots are close in value (especially negative numbers), students make errors. Always visualize them on a number line. Remember that -3 is GREATER than -5.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Comparing only one root of x with one root of y. 2. Forgetting that a negative number with a larger magnitude is actually smaller (e.g., saying -8 > -2). 3. Wasting time dividing by 'a' and dealing with fractions instead of cross-multiplying.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 2 is about comparison speed. Master the 5 options. If you spot opposing inequality signs during comparison, mark CND and move on. Use cross-multiplication of coefficients to avoid fractional comparisons.

tricks.title: The 'Double Negative Constant' Rule (Instant CND)
tricks.explanation: If BOTH equations have a negative constant term ('c' is negative in both), the roots for both will have (+, -) signs. When comparing (+, -) with (+, -), the relationship can NEVER be established. Mark CND in 2 seconds.
tricks.example: Eq1: x² + 5x - 14 = 0. Eq2: y² - 3y - 10 = 0. Both end in a minus. Answer: Cannot be determined.

tricks.title: The Free Comparison (Sign Only Rule)
tricks.explanation: If Eq1 gives roots (+, +) and Eq2 gives roots (-, -), you do NOT need to calculate the actual numbers. Any positive number is greater than any negative number.
tricks.example: Eq1: x² - 5x + 6 = 0 (Roots +,+). Eq2: y² + 7y + 12 = 0 (Roots -,-). Without factoring, x > y.

tricks.title: The Anti-Fraction (Cross-Multiply) Trick
tricks.explanation: To avoid fractions: Let Eq1 be 3x² - 10x + 8 = 0 (factors 6, 4). Let Eq2 be 2y² - 7y + 6 = 0 (factors 4, 3). Instead of roots being 6/3 and 4/2, multiply x's factors by 2, and y's factors by 3.
tricks.example: x factors (6, 4) * 2 = 12, 8. y factors (4, 3) * 3 = 12, 9. Compare: 12=12, 12>9, 8<12. Opposing signs found (>, <). Answer: CND.

tricks.title: The Linear vs Quadratic Match
tricks.explanation: Sometimes you get x² = 25 and y = √25. Remember: Even powers give two roots (+, -). Odd roots give one root (+).
